utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that could be put on the overhead, please? (To the witness): Looking at this exhibit then, before 18th May 1992 the 5th Corps fell under the second army command in Sarajevo, General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as of 10th January 992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to that, the 5th Corps had belonged to the 1st Military District in Belgrade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the control of the 1st Military District in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then the second army command went to the JNA General Staff under the command of General Adzic before 18th May 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Always the units were under the command of the General Staff, so nothing changed there. The 1st Military District and 2nd Military District were under the command of the Chief of the General Staff, General Blagoje Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this document the double red Xs under the name of General Kukanjac indicate that he is a Serb officer from Serbia or Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Serb from Serbia, from Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, General Adzic, is he also a Serbian officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Adzic is from Bosnia, Gacko, Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is he a Serb officer, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Both Kukanjac and General Adzic are active duty officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to offer another exhibit. This would be Prosecution Exhibit 174 for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just ask what is the relevance of whether the officer is an active duty officer or a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance is that, according to the witness's testimony, active duty officers continue to be paid by Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And reserve? We will have an enquiry on that, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): I might ask you, Colonel Selak, you indicated that active duty officers were paid by Belgrade even after 18th May; reserve officers were paid by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Reserve officers by paid by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reserve officers and military conscripts were paid by the government of the Republika Srpska. There was disagreement and dissatisfaction among the officers because the reserve officers were paid far less, something like 50 marks equivalent was the payment of the reserve officer of the rank of Major; whereas an active Major had five or six times that because he was paid by Yugoslavia, and there was dissatisfaction as a result among the men.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would like to ask that this document be marked Prosecution Exhibit 174 for identification, and provide it to the witness. This would be document 17 in the order of documents.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: (To the witness): Sir, does this document indicate the chain of command from the Banja Luka Corps upwards after 18th May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that could be put on the overhead, please? Your Honour, at this time I would tender Prosecution Exhibit 174.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 174 will be admitted. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): Sir, looking at this chain of command after 18th May 1992, again the double red Xs indicate a Serb officer from Serbia or Montenegro, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The officers on this chart, are all three of these officers active duty officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This dotted red line going from the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ army in Belgrade down to the VRS command, does that dotted line indicate that there was no formal chain of command between these two positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was no real chain of command because officially the Commander of the army of the Republika Srspka was Colonel General Ratko Mladic. So this is just pro forma because other relations between the Chief of Staff, the main staff of the Yugoslav Army and the main staff of the army of the Republika Srspka were not really existing but, in fact, they did co-ordinate. This line shows direct a direct line of command between Colonel General Ratko Mladic and the 1st Krajina Corps of which the Commander was General Major Momir Talic. At the time he was Major General; now he is Lieutenant General.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: General Mladic is a Bosnian-Serb officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions now about the 5th Corps's area of operations prior to 18th May and after 18th May. I would ask that this document be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 175 for identification. For the Defence reference, this is map 3. (Exhibit 175 was handed to the witness). Is this the area of responsibility for the Banja Luka Corps before 18th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would tender this as Prosecution Exhibit 175.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 175 will be admitted. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): Looking at this exhibit, the towns that are noted within the area of responsibility, are these the towns to which you have provided Logistics supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You provided Logistics supplies to 5th Corps units within these towns, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to those regions, not necessarily the units within those towns themselves, but they were on location, on location within those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So the actual area of responsibility for the 5th Corps could be somewhat broader than these towns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I noticed that you are providing Logistics support to 5th Corps units in Croatia in Rajic, Pakrac and Nova Gradiska. To your knowledge, were these 5th Corps units in Croatia involved in the combat against the Croats there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I could show you the next Prosecution Exhibit in line which would be Prosecution Exhibit 176 for identification? This will be map 4. (Exhibit 176 was handed to the witness). Colonel Selak, is this the area of responsibility for the 5th Corps as it expanded after 18th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would tender that exhibit as Prosecution Exhibit 176.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 176 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If that could be put on the overhead, please? (To the witness): Colonel Selak, I notice that on this exhibit there are no longer any units in Croatia. The 5th Corps which is, I see now, the 1st Krajina Corps, had those units been withdrawn from Croatia at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you show us, please, the area where the 5th Corps's area of responsibility expanded after 18th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area of responsibility expanded towards the towns of Teslic, Doboj, Modrica, Bosanski Brod, east of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This expansion was the result of combat against what ethnic groups in those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Against Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would ask that that exhibit be retrieved and provided to the Registrar. (To the witness): Sir, I would like to ask you some questions about combat activities and authorisations for combat within the JNA. Within the JNA, what authorisations were necessary to commit military units to combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The state of war could be proclaimed only by the Assembly of the SFRY and if it cannot meet, then the presidency of SFRY. That is the only body authorised to proclaim a state of emergency -- a state of war, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Once a state of war is proclaimed, who has the authority to actually commit military units to combat in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to war plans, the Chief Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army, the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That order would then flow down to the subordinate units who were to execute that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order would go down to the army command, and each army command would issue orders regulating the tasks of subordinate units and he would pass on only those orders that applied to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would happen to a combat unit commander who committed his units to combat without receiving the appropriate authorisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would immediately be replaced and tried by a military Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If such action were taken against a combat Commander, would such action become known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to 18th May 1992, to your knowledge, did any of the combat units within the 5th Corps area of responsibility take part in attacks on non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to May 18th?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It occurred, the Corps was executing combat operations on Croatian territory in Pakrac, Lipik, Nova Gradiska near Jasenovac, west of Pakrac and Lipik.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prior to 18th May 1992, to your knowledge, did JNA units within the 5th Corps area of responsibility take part in attacks on non-Serb areas in Bosnia Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That area is located where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That area is south of Banja Luka, about 120 kilometres on the road Banja Luka/Split.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Against what ethnic groups would the Corps have been involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Against Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, on or after 18th May 1992, to your knowledge, did military units in the 5th Corps have any involvement in attacks on non-Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me first mention Kozarac near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What units were involved in the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps of Banja Luka, it is Motorized Brigade 364 from Prijedor, Light Brigades from Sanski Most and Bosanski Dubica were directly engaged in combat near Prijedor or, rather, in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Just now you mentioned a Motorized Brigade 364 from Prijedor. You had earlier mentioned the 3 ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is a Mechanized Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, how did you learn that these units were involved in the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We supplied those units with food, ammunition and, therefore, I was familiar with the units that were in those positions which we supplied with food and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall on 27th May being present at a briefing at which the attack on Kozarac was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had to report to the Commander of the 1st Krajina Corps in Nova Gradiska, in the building of the penitentiary in Croatia when Colonel Marcetic, Dragan, Chief of the educational body of the Corps command and who was on duty for that day in the Corps, and he informed the Corps Commander, General Talic, that on that day 800 people had been killed or, rather, died in Kozarac and that 1,200 had been captured. There was a minor incident that occurred in connection with that report because I was the only Muslim present at the meeting and in Kozarac there were only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was this incident that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Talic heard the report on the killed number of casualties. Subconsciously, he looked at me and asked Colonel Marcetic: "I suppose you mean 80 people, and put that down in the report". Unfortunately, the fact is that on that day more than 2,000 Muslims were killed in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now when the Colonel -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You might note it says "807" rather than "80".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (To the witness): Colonel Selak, when you testified you indicated that General Talic said to Colonel Marcetic: "I suppose you mean 80 people"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 80, 80, and that he should put that in the report.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When Colonel Marcetic was giving his report, did he also report on soldiers who were injured or killed on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he said four soldiers had been killed and 15 soldiers injured.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you hear any discussion on that date about the direct involvement of the 343rd Brigade in that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no discussion because it was known which units were located there. We knew that it was the area of responsibility of the Mechanized Unit and the Brigades attached for that particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, if tanks and APCs were involved in the attack on Kozarac on this date in May, who would have had control over those tanks and APCs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The leader of the assignment had to be a Mechanized Brigade. A part of those units were near Bosanska Gradiska on duty in facing Croatia, but the bulk of the forces of that Brigade and this combat Brigade were in Prijedor or, rather, Kozarac. Kozarac belongs to the Local Commune of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So those tanks and APCs would have been under the control of the military of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If artillery or cannon were used against Kozarac, who would have been in control of those artillery or cannon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A direct Commander of the combat units was Major Zeljaja Radmilo who, after the capture of Kozarac, the Serbs renamed it to "Radmilovo" after Major Radmilo Zeljaja, in his honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Major Zeljaja was an active duty or a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Active duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he is from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you indicated earlier that Colonel Arsic was the Commander of the 343rd Brigade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: He was an active duty officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So at the time of this attack on Kozarac both he and Major Zeljaja would have been receiving their pay from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, in order for the 343rd to have been committed to combat in the Kozarac area from whom would they have had to receive approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exclusively from the Corps Commander and no-one else; only the Corps Commander could order the use of brigades.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That would at that time have been General Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As an active duty officer, General Talic at that time would have been receiving pay from Belgrade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- he is still receiving it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, if you are going to move into another area, would you help me and put on either the elmo or the overhead projector the exhibit that showed those officers, the three officers, please, and the connection in terms of the logistic contribution? I think it may have been -- I thought it was 174, but it is before then.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You want the 5th Corps chain of command after 18th May?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, not the 5th Corps chain of command, that I have. It is the 5th Corps and then Mladic, and above that, that is the dotted line. That is 174. But there should be one before that that would show all of these people -- no?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: There is a 5th Corps chain of command before which would show General Talic ---

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- would show Colonel Arsic; it did not show Major Zeljaja who was a subordinate to Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What exhibit is that?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The one that shows the chain of command after 18th May is 172.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I see that, please?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes. (Exhibit 172 was handed to the witness). If you could show the top of it showing General Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now what we are talking about now is the attack on Kozarac. At that time you say that the Major would have been -- well, you go ahead and ask the questions and see if you can locate the people.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Certainly. (To the witness): You have indicated that the Commander of the 343rd Brigade at that time was Colonel Arsic, is that correct? Could the exhibit be moved up so that that is shown. This here says the 43rd Mechanized Brigade. Is that different than the 343rd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the figure "3" was removed; I do not know for what reason. It is the same Brigade. Just one number is missing, 3, 343; I do not know for what reason, but that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Commander of this Brigade at the time of the attack on Kozarac was Colonel Arsic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Major Zeljaja, what was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was Chief of Staff and Deputy Brigade Commander.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: To Colonel Arsic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right. On this chain of command, I note that there are arrows going from the combat units around the side here of the exhibit and up to General Talic. Does this indicate that General Talic would have direct chain of command authority over the combat commands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been arbitrariness if Colonel Arsic were to commit the unit without the knowledge and approval of his superior Commander, so that General Talic certainly knew and approved the commitment of these brigades.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So let me try to make my question more clear: Would you look at this exhibit, please, and you see the arrows going from General Talic down directly to the Corps combat units? Does this signify that for operational matters these combat units went directly to General Talic in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, let me clarify. The Corps command plans combat operations on the basis of the ideas of the Corps command. When they planned those combat operations, the Commander takes a decision on the commitment of units and he alone can order the commitment of units.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Both of those gentlemen are Bosnian Serbs, is that correct, if I understand your exhibit correctly?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the testimony was he thinks that Colonel Arsic is from Serbia, but it was not marked that way because he is not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He just says the accent makes him believe that he is from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. However, General Talic is a Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Were both of those officers active officers before May 18th 1992?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Were they active officers after May 18th 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That means, according to your testimony, they received their pay from Belgrade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am quite sure because I myself received my pension from Belgrade until May last year, and all other officers living in Banja Luka received our pensions from Belgrade; just as the same pension that a Colonel had in Belgrade, I had in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge McDonald, does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, it does. I apologise for interrupting but it is important for me to understand it now rather than having to go back and look at all the exhibits without the Colonel with me. So we will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, would you like to continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Colonel Selak, before the break we were talking about 27th May meeting at which the attack on Kozarac was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that meeting do you recall General Talic making a comment that Muslims were dying because of Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was that comment made, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was during a meeting when General Talic heard a report of Colonel Dragan Blaskic about the casualties in Kozarac, about people being killed. He said that Muslims were dying because of the Croats and their policy towards the Serbs. I cannot remember the details, but the gist of it was that the Muslims were dying because of the Croats, because they had sided with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Because the Muslims had sided with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, we have spoken before about your leaving your active duties in mid-July 1992, and that was because of your retirement, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who actually approved your retirement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order, my retirement was signed by the Ministry of National Defence of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could ask that the next exhibit in line be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 177 for identification? For Defence purposes, this would be document 7. (Exhibit 177 was handed to the witness).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have the Yugoslav text on the elmo while the witness is identifying it so also our client can see it?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any problem with that, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I do note, your Honour, that this exhibit is both in Serbo-Croatian and with an English translation. (To the witness): Colonel Selak, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the order No. 6-114 of the Ministry of the Defence of the army of Yugoslavia of 30th June '92 on the termination of my active duty.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Minister of the Defence of the army of Yugoslavia, is this the army located in Belgrade or is this the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army from Belgrade, the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is the effective date of the termination of your service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 30th September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would tender Prosecution Exhibit 177.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 177 will be admitted. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): So then, Colonel Selak, you were, in effect, retired from the army of Yugoslavia, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This document indicates that your service actually terminated on 30th September 1992. You have indicated that you left your active duty position about 10th July 1992. What was your status between 10th July and 30th September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on holidays for three months. It was supposed to start on 1st July, but there was nobody to replace me, and then Colonel Skondric came with the order that he was taking over the post from me and that was on 10th July '92. I merely came to the office from time to time until Colonel Skondric replaced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So this period of leave between relinquishing your active duty position and your retirement, was this a normal procedure in the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the regular retirement, every army officer was entitled to three months of leave plus a month of leave for the current year, so that one could have four months at a stretch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You indicated you were replaced by an officer, Colonel Skondric, I believe you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Skondric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This officer was an active duty or a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Active duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You know where he was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sanski Most, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sir, after you retired did you at some point begin to receive retirement pay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The retirement pay began on November 1st because until I was -- until that time I received my salary and the first retirement pay arrived on November 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Where did you your retirement pay come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to have this document marked as Prosecution Exhibit 178 for identification and this would be document 9. (Exhibit 178 was handed to the witness)

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could we have that on the elmo too, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think all the exhibits you plan to offer, put the Serbian on the elmo so that you do not have to hand it back to Mr. Tadic. That may be your only copy, I suppose. You will do that, will you, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Perhaps the Defence could tell us -- I think it is a two-page document -- if you want the second page on and when. (To the witness): Colonel Selak, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the ruling of the Social -- Military Social Insurance Administration of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That is located where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This was the determination that determined how much retirement pay you would be entitled to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it says on what grounds I was retired, what pay category and all the elements taken into consideration when determining the amount of my pension.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I tender this exhibit as Prosecution Exhibit 178.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 178 will be admitted. MISS HOLLIS (To the witness): So that your retirement pay was determined by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Located in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Proleterskih brigada Street, No. 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If that exhibit then could be returned to the Registrar? Colonel Selak, in July or August 1992 after you relinquished your position as Commander of the 14th Logistics Base, did you become a member of a Muslim resistance group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was your role in the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you ever take up arms against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What were the type of actions that you determined that your group would take to assist Muslims in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All but armed resistance because it was our belief that a massacre of the Muslim people would occur, like the one in Kozarac, because mosques and other objects had been mined during 15 to -- within 15 or 20 days. They wanted the Muslims to offer an armed resistance so that a massacre could take place, and we were against armed resistance in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying were you against "armoured" or "armed" resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Armed resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: After you retired from the military, were you allowed to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who informed you that you could not leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Talic with whom -- who was a good friend of mind before that, invited me in August '92 to his office and informed me that not to think about moving away, moving out, but that nobody would lay a finger on me. I asked him about military authorities. I said, "Military authorities, all right, but what about the police, what about the SDS?" and he said: "I cannot guarantee that, but the army will not lay a finger on you".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you would not be allowed to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not why, but I got the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was the message?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that he thought that I would join the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and prevented that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you indicated that you eventually left Banja Luka in 1995, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on May 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you have to make any type of arrangements or payments in order to leave Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife was gravely ill and she had to have a colon operated for a tumour. The doctors behaved very correctly. They were all Serbs. It took place in 94, but in 95 her health deteriorated. The tumour was a malignant one and the team of physicians in Banja Luka clinical centre issued a recommendation for her treatment in Belgrade. However, Colonel Manjanovic, doctor, head of the Medical Corps in Banja Luka, did not want to drive her, and because of that I telephoned to some military commanders asking for help, and they did not want to. I paid 2,800 marks to two Serbs to take me to Belgrade in their car. I spent 14 days in Belgrade asking for permission to go to Germany. The German Embassy issued an entry visa to me and only after 14 days was I given the permission to leave Yugoslavia because my son has sent guarantee, so I went my wife to Germany where she underwent an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Sir, what was the result of that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Death.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, I am going to ask you some questions on an entirely different matter. The first thing I would like you to look at is something that you may be familiar with and that is a military book. Mr. Usher, could you hand this to the witness, please? There is a military book. If you look inside the front cover you will see it is in the name of "Dusko Tadic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can take it, Colonel, that you are familiar with documents such as these, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document comes from the Prosecution and copies have been made so that we may have a look at it together. If I can ask Mr. Bos or Mr. Usher to -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You wish to offer this and there will be no objection, I gather, as to authenticity or will there be, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There will not be any objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you wish to offer it, what number will that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Defence 7.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, what is your position regarding this military book?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would certainly have no objection to its authenticity. To the extent this is beyond the scope of direct examination, we would not object to allowing it to happen because of time for this witness. He would not have to be recalled. So to the extent this may go beyond direct, we have no objection to that either.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The bottom line, regardless of whether it is beyond or not, there is no objection. If you wish to offer it, then I gather no objection.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no objection. This may be Defence Exhibit 8.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I made a mistake. I said 7 and I did not have a list before me; it was just my memory which is not the best. Are you offering then Defence Exhibit 8 and let us have an identification of it for the record, please? There is no objection and it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is the military book of Dusko Tadic. Perhaps a copy could be put before the witness so that I may have the original back with me?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Actually, Miss Hollis, I do not know that I could rule as to whether it was beyond cross (sic) until I understand what is in it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Exactly, your Honour. I simply wanted to make it clear that to the extent it was beyond direct, we would not object.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Beyond direct, excuse me, yes. Very good. It is admitted then. MR. KAY (To the witness): Perhaps if we look at the second page in our bundle -- everyone has copies now -- and it records Mr. Tadic's name with his photograph, is that correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the military book that is issued or was issued in the former Yugoslavia to those who were called up for military service, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is off, I have been told. The pages have been photocopied here, perhaps slightly out of sequence, but we see his date of birth recorded originally as 1st September 1955 and an amendment has taken place recording it as 1st October, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the place of Kozarac, the opstina of Prijedor and in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dates are recorded, 19th February, I think it is 1975 but there is a stamp obscuring it on the inside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of this page in section 1 there is a date that is recorded of, I believe it is, 14th October 1976 in the left-hand stamp, and in the right hand stamp in that section 1, 28th February 1977. Can you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the original before me these are stamps that have been signed. Perhaps you could tell us what information would be recorded here within the military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These -- this is information about the period of service in the Yugoslav People's Army from 1976 to 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Every conscript who undertakes this kind of service would have these stamps put in their military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In section 2 beneath that, we have a stamp with a date in the left-hand stamp of 1st March 1977 to 28th November 1977, and again both stamps have been signed. Would this record, similarly, military service during those periods of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. I do not know. Perhaps he was ill and then was discharged, because here is one year of military service. I do not know what happened. Perhaps he was attending a drill or a training as a military. I am not sure. I am not sure what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The period of time we are dealing with there, however, is 1977?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning to the next page in our bundle at the top of the page, which is recorded as page 5 and column 5, in that first box there with the date of 19th October 1973, a stamp with a signature, again what information would be recorded here in the military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the information about the time when he was drafted for regular military service, and it says "fit for military service" and a signature of the relevant authority, and a stamp, it was with headquarters in Banja Luka for the Secretariat for National Defence authorised for these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page, which is a different page in the book, however, we see on section 7 again a stamp, there is not in fact a date with it, but there is the word "radio-mekanicar", and a number. What would that indicate, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that he was drafted for technical service, radio mechanic. I see this figure here, something 28, this would be, this is the special branch, the speciality. That is how it is coded in the army for radio mechanics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next page and, in fact, we have no stamps there. These pages, Colonel, which are without stamp, what would be the kind of information that would normally be recorded, perhaps taking the left-hand section first on page 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps someone could assist the witness and put the right channel on? I know the feeling! I will repeat the question. Page 10. There we have a succession of blank pages. Have you got it there? It is a blank sheet page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What kind of information would be recorded on the top left-hand section on page 10 of the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldier of the completion of military service, it is a wartime assignment in JNA units or TO units, and every unit has training or drills of the reserve troops from time to time; and whenever a person is called up it needs to be recorded, the dates from when until then a person underwent an exercise, and then the signature of the Commander of the unit of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So, if you undertake training within the TO or the JNA, this information would be recorded on this page in the military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the next section, still on that page, however, Colonel ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- if you can remain on the same page because, in fact, there is a different heading on pages 12 and 13, "Vojna Vezba". What kind of information would be recorded on this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see here first -- oh, you mean No. 10? Yes, this is the wartime assignment in State Security station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have actually jumped ahead of us, Colonel. If I can stop you there and take you back to the previous page which was where my -- if you just follow me through the pages rather than turning ahead, we will arrive at the same place, hopefully. Turn over that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turn over that page. Have you got a blank page there showing pages 12 and 13 of the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10, 12 and 13, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could hand it to me?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The pages are on the bottom, Colonel, do you see these numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have been in French and we have got lost and now we are, hopefully, in the right place. Please do not turn over the pages until I say, otherwise we will get lost. Can you see "Vojna Vezba" there on pages 12 and 13 as they would be in the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What kind of information would be recorded on these pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the information about the date when a person has been summoned for a drill, when the drill was over, how long he had spent, the signature and a stamp of the authorised body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have here a blank page; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning over now to the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. 13 or 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you see there the section of the book dealing with pages 14 and 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 14 is actually a continuation of what we had seen before, but on page 15 there we have a new section 10 and perhaps you could tell us ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- what this section 10 on page 15 records?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It records the participation of the soldier in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In war? How does that come to be recorded in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is special kind of information on the basis of one's participation in war, individuals become entitled to certain rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The SJB Prijedor, what does the "SJB" stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Station of Public Security Prijedor. This is the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is the civil police, and we have two dates within the stamps there, 16th June 1992 on the left-hand side ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and 25th December 1992 on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not '95, it is '92, I think. It must be "2" in the end, not "5", in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Hopefully that is what I had said and, as I look at the transcript, I said 1992 -- which shows the period of service commencing and the period of service ending in the civil police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In box (2) beneath that there is a further stamp, 10th June 1993, and what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the date when he was admitted to a new military unit, new wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can just move now to further down that page, page 16, where we have got a title to a new page, what does that show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is column 11 in military records, Municipal Assembly of Prijedor of 28th December '71.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 1971, and what does it indicate within this column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it indicates that a conscript is on the records of the Secretariat for National Defence and that he is kept on their books as of that date; that as of that date he becomes a conscript under the law of National Defence, that he has to report at a given time when he is called up by the military authorities to the place which he is assigned to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is on that date that you enter into the records as they would have been for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us move to the next page, blank sections, but if we look at pages 20 and 21 as they have got on the foot of the page, can you see those? First of all, what kind of information would be entered on page 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, on the replacement of the military book, if it is replaced, then in the old book it must be noted that he has received a new book, and in column 13 that his military obligation of that person has ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On page 21 where we have some formal text, I do not want you to translate it, but can you just tell us what is contained within section (14) of the military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In section (14) the rights and obligations of conscripts are indicated, and it is explicitly stated what are his rights and his obligations, to remind him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As we turn over a page now to pages 22 and 23, again those rights are repeated, is that right, and on page 24?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the next section we cannot see anything reproduced on page 25, but if we turn over the page to pages 26 and 27 of the book, these are coupons that are in the back of the book, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What are these coupons for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those coupons said that on the basis of his wartime assignment he has immediately to report to his military unit, and it indicates the exact mobilization place which has already been announced to him and which he has visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And these coupons are torn out of the book, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They are in perforated sections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The rest of the book is reproduced here without any further entries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could I retrieve the original of that document for purposes of questioning, please? Colonel Selak, on page 15 of that document do you see the stamps that appear there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you able to read those stamps to determine what agency stamped those pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first two stamps I cannot decipher from the photocopy, but these are small stamps, or small in diameter, which were indeed used by the public security service in the opstinas. This third stamp is the stamp of the military postal code. I cannot read the number, but it says Vojna Posta 7288. I believe this must be the wartime number of the units to which he has been assigned. The war number does need not coincide with the number of the peace time military post. Each unit had a wartime code as well which only that unit was familiar with and its superior command.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, you said that two of these stamps appear to be public security services stamps. Is that the civilian police you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: May I confer for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps because these copies are so hard to read and the stamps are difficult, I realise this is a Defence exhibit, but perhaps the original would be the best exhibit to provide to the Court for your examination. Should you wish to examine it later this would be much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely no objection, your Honour, and the reproduction is poor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Then we will make the original Defence Exhibit 8.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask that the original document be given to Colonel Selak. It is open at pages 14 and 15. I think perhaps we could put just that page on the elmo and bend the book. If you are looking at section 10 part 1 where the letters 0D appear, what is the date that you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16 of the 6th 1992, 16th June.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now that you have the opportunity to look at these stamps and the original, are these in fact civilian police stamps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So does that indicate that the entries would have been made and then approved by the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And this would have been the civilian police in Prijedor, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Attached to the Security Centre Banja Luka because they were subordinated to the Security Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then if I could retrieve the original document, please. Perhaps just to assist the Court, I know that reference was made to page 25, it was unclear on the copies what page 25 actually looks like. Could that perhaps be shown so that page 25 shows coupons missing, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions to ask of the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Colonel, I wanted to ask you something to clarify a matter that I am not clear on. Assume a young man, say 20, in the 1980s he would have been subject to conscription in the ordinary course of events into the JNA, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Assuming he is healthy, fit, how would he ever end up in the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the completion of his military service in the Yugoslav People's Army when he returns from his unit he would have to report within 48 hours to the Secretariat for National Defence of the Municipal Assembly where he resides. His file from the unit is sent by official mail to his municipality. If he does not report, he is called in directly so that he cannot avoid receiving war time assignment in the Secretariat for National Defence where he resides.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Well, assuming a time of peace and he has done his military service in the JNA and then is discharged, he automatically goes into the TO or does he volunteer to serve in the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he does not state his view. Service in the Yugoslav People's Army is training according to specialities, ranging from infantry, artillery, depending for which branch he was recruited. When he completes that training, and that lasts up to one year, early on it was 15 months and even two years, and in 1983 a new law on military service for men of 18 years of age was 15 months. When he returns home, when he is discharged, he is distributed into the war time units of the Yugoslav People's Army according to the specialities for which he has been trained, and only those people who are surplus were given to the Territorial Defence. Similarly, the ranks of the Security Services were filled in. They were given certain people at their request or in other ways to fill in the wartime Police Force.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So does that mean that this young man that we are thinking of, having finished his compulsory military service, either remains as a reserve soldier or else if not wanted as a reserve soldier and being surplus to requirements, then automatically goes into the TO, is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That classifies that. The second thing I wanted to ask you was, you have made reference in your evidence to the Second Military District in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The headquarters were or was in Sarajevo of that district?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the headquarters of the Second Military District was in Sarajevo as of January 10th '92 until it collapsed, I think it was in May '92.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Although in Sarajevo it of course had no connection, I assume, with the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was directly subordinated to the General Staff of the Yugoslav People's Army in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It was not in Pale which is very close to Sarajevo; it was in Sarajevo itself, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo itself there is a command building headquarters of the previously Seventh Army. In '88 there was a reorganisation of the Yugoslav People's Army and army districts were formed, and the Seventh Army was disbanded and they were subjected to the military command in Belgrade. With the formation of the Second Army the command was again located in those buildings in the city of Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But presumably in no way under the control of the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The last question I wanted to ask you was that in the course of your evidence, as I understood it, you said that on 15th May 1992 those soldiers who had been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina were ordered to report and place themselves at the disposal of JNA units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that they were directly ordered to join, what, specified JNA units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had to report, those from units doing their military service in various places like Macedonia or elsewhere, they had to go to specific units. About 105 soldiers came to me from Yugoslavia, young men born in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Bosnian Krajina, mostly in Banja Luka. I do not know whether they were asked where they wanted to go or where they were born. Probably that is how they were returned. I did not ask them, but they all had to report to units in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that JNA soldiers who on 15th May or thereabouts 1992 were born in Serbia and Montenegro and serving in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were ordered to report to units outside Bosnia-Herzegovina; that was one class of soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then another class were those who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were ordered to report to some units of the JNA within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions, Colonel. The Defence Exhibit 8 was identified as a military book for Mr. Tadic. What does that mean? Does that mean that -- well, explain to me what it means? What is a military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A military book serves as a document for the military conscript, as an ID card, and it has validity in the unit. It is the only document with which he proves his identity.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So when he either is joined or invited to join into the military, he is given this book? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then I gather in this book is stamped the position, the office that he holds and the length of time that he holds that office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So if I were then to look at Defence 8 I could determine then every position that Mr. Tadic had in the military, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on condition that the Secretariat and the unit were up-to-date.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What does that mean? What do you mean up-to-date? That they did their job properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But you indicated that on page 25 there were some coupons missing, if you look at the original, and then when you were responding to questions concerning page 26 you described coupons as stating the wartime assignment and military unit to which he must report. So my question is, since there are some coupons missing, can I truly determine from looking at this book every military assignment Mr. Tadic held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Probably that is not a well-stated question. Can I determine from looking at this book every military position Mr. Tadic held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then what is the purpose of the coupons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of the coupons is that he must report to a lower unit. The records are kept at the level of a Brigade, Battalion Brigades, and in the coupon there is a number saying where he has to report to a lower level unit, a company or a detachment, and he carries this coupon saying where he is assigned because he does not know until he is told that at the Mobilization Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So when the stamps are made that indicates the positions that he has held and the coupons are used by him to go to wherever the assignment is, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, where he is assigned to. (No translation).

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I am not hearing the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His company leader knew to what posts he had assigned him. It is not indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These entries I gather were made, some of them were made at a time when there was a mobilization and persons were called into the service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If someone was appointed to an office, for example, Secretary of a Local Commune, and if that satisfied his mobilization obligation, would that have been entered in this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would say that he has a new assignment, that he has been assigned to civilian protection, the police station or that he has been discharged because of sickness or some other reason.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That would be one of these stamps that you have indicated that are on the various pages, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Not one of the missing coupons that I did not understand. It is one of the stamps that I would have to take a look at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, if he is relieved then there is a special column and he is deleted from the records.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And where would that be? Where would I look for that in this book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 20 column 13.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That would indicate if someone was relieved from the military for emergency reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may be relieved because of disease or old age, because if he became a conscript at 18 it lasts until he is 60, on the basis of sickness or changing his place of residence, if he is moving to another commune, another municipality or to another state, if he is changing his place of residence. There are many reasons for which this wartime assignment is deleted or if he is going abroad for employment.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In your testimony you indicated regarding Exhibits 170 and 174 that there are some dotted lines. Do you recall these organisational charts? Can you see them from here generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: There were some dotted lines going from the VRS command looking at 170 to the Logistics Administration with various individuals, and you had indicated that the dotted lines meant that there was no formal chain of command but that there was a co-ordination between the two. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said that even though there was no formal chain of command there was a co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I can speak of my own unit. I regularly had contacts and my subordinates with the Technical Administration of the Army of Yugoslavia and with the Base of the Technical Administration of the Army of Yugoslavia in Belgrade. My bodies also contacted with other units, other Bases in Belgrade, Novi Sad, Ceugic concerning essential supplies for my Base. By way of example I had contacts with Colonel Brkic Milisav, Commander of the Technical Administration based in Belgrade for critical supplies which I was short of. So there was no direct command, chain of command, but there was this communication on what was necessary. My transport were regularly going from Banja Luka to the territory of Yugoslavia where they received the necessary materiel, supplies and equipment for my Base.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So I am referring to Exhibit 170 which indicates that this would have been have been after May 18th 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Just a few, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, I believe you indicated in response to Judge McDonald questions about the accused's military book that the information she asked about would be in the book if the book had been kept up-to-date, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So if for some reason the book had not been kept current, then such information would not be in the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now the Second Military District that was headquartered in Sarajevo, that Second Military District was under the command of the Yugoslav Army, the JNA, headquartered in Belgrade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Second Military District was at no time under the command of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You also indicated that as of a certain date in May there was an order that Bosnian-Serb soldiers who were out of Bosnia must return to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that soldiers who were not Bosnian Serbs must leave Bosnia, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now to your knowledge, if we are talking about soldiers, not officers, to your knowledge as of that date in May did all the Serb soldiers who were from Serbia in fact leave Bosnia and go back to Serbia or Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can talk about my unit. From my unit they did. I also believe they did from Corps units because their parents had intervened asking for the boys to come back because they feared for their lives, so they did return. Whether somebody stayed behind of his own will, I do not know, but he could if he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So these were Serb soldiers who were from Serbia or Montenegro left Bosnia and returned to Serbia or Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not Serbs only. There were Albanians, Montenegrins, Muslims or Bosniaks. That is all those born in that territory, that is the territory of Montenegro or Serbia could go back. They were Hungarians from Vojvodina, that is all those who were doing their military service in the territory of, in the units in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you testified earlier that contrary to what happened with the soldiers, most of the Serb officers you knew who were from Serbia or Montenegro in fact remained in Bosnia after this date, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they stayed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Concerning conscripts who had completed their mandatory active service, you indicated that they would first be assigned to the JNA reserves once the JNA reserves were filled and then they would go to the Territorial Defence Forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not mention that wartime units, rather the JNA units, were entitled to a 5 per cent more of a replenishment than the original formation, that is when they would be filled up to 105 per cent of the wartime strength, then the rest of the men could be assigned to TO or I do not know if they were physicians, then to hospitals or to military industries and so on and so forth. There were cases of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Some of these overflow, if you will, of reservists could also be assigned to reserve militia units, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: And by "militia" here I mean civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could turn to the part of the military book dealing with pages 14 and 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where the stamp of the civil police is included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those dates of 16th June 1992 to 25th December 1992 appear to be stamps current for that period, beginning of the service on 16th June, finish of the service on 25th December, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So for that period at least the book was kept up-to-date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection then to Colonel Selak being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Then, Colonel Selak, you are permanently excused. Thank you very much for coming. You may leave. (The witness withdrew). I want to talk with Counsel. Mr. Wladimiroff, we I guess last week talked about the schedule in July. You had indicated that you did want to make arrangements to continue discovery. I know it is difficult for you because you have to make them well in advance. I told you I was having some difficulty because until a Judge of Trial Chamber Two (sic) actually submits the indictments to the entire Trial Chamber for a Rule 61 hearing, there is no assurance that it is going to happen. I have spoken with a member of the Trial Chamber and they firmly believe that they will go forward with that Rule 61 proceeding. So even though that order has not been entered, that is what they have told me. So I think that it is safe, I know that it is safe for you -- I say I know -- I believe it is safe for you ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Almost safe!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- to make arrangements to go where you need to go to complete your discovery. So we will not then be hearing the case for the first two weeks of July and June 27th and 28th. So the first two weeks then of July is what we are planning on the other Trial Chamber having its Rule 61 proceeding and so we will not be hearing this case, nor will we hear it on 27th and 28th. They will begin the Rule 61 proceeding on 27th I am told. So we will make arrangements accordingly. If I hear anything further I will tell you as soon as I hear something. Mr. Niemann, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I know disappointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We may have some questions left, if I may?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So that means that from 27th June up to 12th of July there will be no hearing in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, sir

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right. I take it that the other dates in June and July will be the regular Tuesday up to Friday hearings, unless it is given notice that that will not apply?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I also heard, true or not true, that there will be another biannual meeting of the Judges on 24th and 25th or 25th and 26th. If that is true I take it you will not sit either?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No. We have decided that this case is more important, and so we are not attending that plenary meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So I have not heard it!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have heard that there is a meeting, you are very correct. Sometimes you hear things faster than I do, but we have decided that we will not attend, that this is more important. Very good. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10 o'clock.

procedural_notes.text: (The hearing adjourned until the following day)
